claims.text: Superconducting transition temperature in high-entropy superconducting alloys is governed by enhanced electron–phonon coupling.
Large atomic-size mismatch in high-entropy compositions produces local lattice strain.
Local lattice strain caused by atomic-size mismatch enhances electron–phonon coupling.
A broad distribution of atomic sizes produces significant local lattice distortions.
The baseline high-entropy alloy has a high superconducting transition temperature.
Replacing constituents with elements of more similar atomic size will reduce local lattice strain.
The substitution can be performed while keeping the overall electron count roughly constant.
Metallicity is required for the proposed electron–phonon-mediated superconducting response.
Atomic-size mismatch causes phonon softening through local lattice distortion.
Softened phonon modes increase electron–phonon coupling.
Local lattice distortions elevate the density of states at the Fermi level.
Increased electron–phonon coupling and an elevated Fermi-level density of states raise the superconducting transition temperature.
Reducing atomic-size mismatch will decrease the electron–phonon coupling constant relative to the baseline alloy.
Reducing atomic-size mismatch will lower the superconducting transition temperature relative to the baseline alloy.
The baseline alloy exhibits robust superconductivity and significant atomic-size disparity.
The proposed mechanism applies only where electron–phonon interactions dominate superconducting pairing.
Magnetic or spin-fluctuation-mediated pairing could obscure the effect of reduced atomic-size mismatch.
Inelastic neutron scattering or Raman spectroscopy can be used to determine the relevant phonon spectra and electron–phonon coupling parameters.
An unchanged transition temperature despite a significant reduction in atomic-size disparity would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
